clone_cost.note: our estimate with assumptions visible; not a claim about the team

assumptions: a wiki or knowledge base with a review workflow you can post diffs into (MediaWiki pending changes, or a PR-style flow)
a per-claim research budget, since a pass costs a search plus several model calls for every claim on the page
a decision about contested facts: staff the disagreement bucket, or suppress that category rather than flood maintainers
value.estimate: 2-3 weeks — the ledger is the project, the model calls are glue
value.why: The walkthrough is ordinary orchestration over two APIs: extract, prioritise, research, judge, draft, cross-check, render a diff. What takes the time is the claim ledger — extracting claims reliably, keying them so a re-run recognises the same claim in a re-edited article, and the due-date and link graph on top — plus the fixture recorder that keeps iteration cheap. The dependency-free core design is what makes the second part cheap to get right.

data_and_models.value: Two vendor APIs with explicit division of labour: Parallel for web research, Gemini for the judgement (still true / changed / sources disagree). Between them a dependency-free Python ledger tracking each claim, its last-checked time, its next due time and its links to other claims; vendor SDKs only at the edges. Stateless service on Cloud Run scaled to zero; the Built With list adds Firestore and pymongo for storage. No model is trained and no accuracy figure is given for either the judge or the researcher.

how_it_works.value: Python backend, plain JavaScript frontend with no framework and no build step, one Cloud Run service that scales to zero. Parallel does the research, Gemini does the judging. The part the author spent the most time on is the ledger: a small dependency-free Python core that tracks every claim, when it was last checked, when it is due next and what else it is connected to. It never touches the network, so the interesting logic is testable without a cloud account or an API key, and the vendor SDKs live only at the edges. Built With additionally names FastAPI, uvicorn, Firestore, pymongo, Docker, Cloud Build and Secret Manager.

how_they_tested.value: A real harness discipline is described rather than measured: the first live run recorded every search result and model response to disk so all later development replayed from fixtures at zero cost, and the ledger core has no dependencies, so most of the test suite runs on a bare Python interpreter with no database, emulator or cloud project. No case count, coverage figure or pass rate is published, there is no evaluation of the judge's accuracy against labelled facts, and no repository is linked, so none of it can be inspected.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Cost. One pass over a single page is a web search per claim plus several Gemini calls, which is fine once and not fine while tuning a prompt forty times in an afternoon. The answer was to record fixtures: the first live run wrote every search result and model response to disk, after which the whole pipeline could replay from them for free — so the classify stage could be rewritten and all stages run end to end at no cost. The same reasoning drove the local-first design: the ledger core has no dependencies at all, so most of the test suite runs on a bare Python interpreter with nothing installed, and the billing meter did not start until the day of deployment.

value.relation: the same shape — a machine ranking facts for a human to act on, deliberately stopping short of acting — and the two pages differ almost entirely on whether the judgement is checkable: Continuity returns old text, new text, a citation and a confidence score per claim, while the fisheries tool returns a risk classification whose own page says there is no ground truth for it.

both convert an unverifiable judgement into an artifact a person can check (a cited diff, a signed finding) and both keep the human as the writer of record; the difference is what they attach evidence to — one grounds a claim against the live web on a schedule, the other against a versioned rule set in CI.

both are staged agent pipelines that publish a dollar figure, and read together they move the number worth tracking: Greenlight quotes cost per run against a measured output, Continuity quotes total build cost and explains that fixtures made every later iteration free — so iteration cost, not run cost, is what decides whether a pipeline is developable.

what_breaks_first.value: The fixed staleness window. 'Skip what was verified last week' is a single guess about decay rates applied uniformly, and it is wrong in both directions for the facts this targets: a film's release date almost never moves, while 'current holder of X' can move in a day — so the budget is spent re-checking stable facts while the volatile ones age out between passes. Second: the reviewer's queue. 'Sources disagree' is a terminal category with no triage described, and on a long contested article it can hold a large share of the claims; a maintainer handed forty cited diffs and thirty unresolved disagreements has been given a new job, not a lighter one.

what_it_does.value: One button on an article page; no setup, config or schedule to configure. The agent reads the page, writes down every factual claim it makes one at a time, decides which are worth checking now (claims verified last week are skipped), researches each on the live web through Parallel, judges what came back with Gemini as still-true, changed or sources-disagree, drafts the edit with the citation attached, cross-checks that edit against the rest of the page so one fixed paragraph cannot contradict another, and hands it back as a diff with old text, new text, sources and a confidence score. Then it stops and waits: approve, rewrite or throw out — nothing reaches the page until a person says so.

what_it_is.value: A MediaWiki companion that re-reads a page fact by fact on a schedule, researches each claim against the live web, and hands the maintainer a cited diff for every fact that quietly stopped being true — never writing to the article itself.

what_to_steal.value: Record fixtures on the first live run — write every search result and model response to disk once, and every later iteration is free; that single habit is what made the whole thing developable on a hackathon budget. Keep vendor SDKs at the edges around a dependency-free core so the interesting logic runs on a bare interpreter with no key. Schedule re-verification per claim with a last-checked and next-due time rather than per page, and keep a link graph between claims so an edit to one paragraph can be checked against its neighbours. And always hand back a diff with citations instead of writing to the system of record.

continuity-g7bty0.name: Continuity
verdict_reasons: soundness 0.50 over 64% of the rubric; 0 named unknown(s) remain → publishable with caveats
continuity-g7bty0.worth_note: The diagnosis is worth more than the demo: a fact that used to be true and quietly stopped being true looks exactly like every correct sentence around it, and nobody edited the page — the world moved on. Treating wiki rot as a decay problem with a per-claim due date instead of an error problem is the right shape, and keeping the human as writer of record (a cited diff, never a publish) is the right posture for public knowledge infrastructure. The write-up also documents its own development discipline in the same breath as the product, which lets a reader check the cost claim against the fixture claim.

built_with_verified.value: declared by the authors (8): dart, flutter, gemini, google-cloud, google-translate, nestjs, postgresql, typescript · no repository published, so these are the team's own claim and nothing corroborates them

clone_cost.note: our estimate with assumptions visible; not a claim about the team

assumptions: the courses and progress state exist independently of the AI layer, since the page describes a pivot onto existing infrastructure rather than a new build
no model is trained or fine-tuned - every AI surface named is a hosted Gemini call - so quality rests on prompting and supplied learner context
translation is machine translation with AI assistance, as no human review or per-market authoring process is described
value.why: Reproducing the described surface is weeks, not days: a Flutter client for two platforms, NestJS over PostgreSQL with learner, course, progress and assessment schemas, four Gemini surfaces (tutor, mentor, quiz generation, feedback), translation wiring, plus the authoring workflow for course content. The months are in what the page does not describe and the market demands - a catalogue that is relevant per market rather than merely translated, grading that can be trusted enough to be called assessment, and an economics answer for inference on a learner's five-minute session over metered data.

data_and_models.value: Learner, course, progress, assessment and application data in PostgreSQL, served by NestJS/Node.js to Flutter clients. Gemini is the model behind tutoring, mentorship, quiz generation and assessment feedback, with Google Cloud Translation for localisation; the personalisation is described as context-driven (goals, activity, lesson content, assessment performance, progress) with no retrieval store, embedding pipeline or fine-tune mentioned. Usage and operational telemetry are captured about the AI features themselves. No evaluation set, rubric, benchmark or grading study is described for the assessment claims, and no learner outcome measure appears on the page. Educational content is authored through 'AI-assisted content workflows', which is where the quality risk sits and is described in five words.

how_it_works.value: Mobile-first, with production Android and iOS applications in Flutter (dart, typescript, QML-free: the page lists flutter/dart), a NestJS and Node.js backend and PostgreSQL for learner, course, progress, assessment and application data. The production AI stack is named as Gemini-powered Tutor, Gemini-powered Mentor, an AI Quiz Studio for generating quizzes and assessments, AI-powered assessment workflows for evaluating learner work, Gemini-assisted personalisation over goals, activity, progress and educational context, and Google Cloud Translation for localisation. Everything is described as built by integrating Gemini into the workflows rather than standing beside them, with the learner's context (goals, course activity, lesson content, assessment performance, progress) supplied to it. AI usage and operational data are captured so the team can monitor performance and see how learners interact with the AI systems. The platform was assembled by pivoting an existing product: LearnWay's infrastructure and content were kept, the AI layer was built new.

how_they_tested.value: Nothing is published: no test suite, no eval harness, no learner pilot, no grading comparison, no A/B of the tutor's usefulness, and no repository to look for any of it. The closest thing to an evidence practice on the page is the stated capture of AI usage and operational data to monitor performance and understand learner interaction, which is a measurement loop pointed at the features rather than at learning outcomes - and no figure from it is reported.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Four, and they are architecture and access rather than model quality. Moving from AI as a feature to AI as part of the operating architecture: a chatbot is easy, but a system that knows what a learner is studying, weighs their progress, guides, evaluates and recommends needs far more context and orchestration. Accessibility: the learners they want to serve rely on smartphones, mobile data, lower-cost devices and inconsistent connectivity, so sophisticated AI had to be balanced against a simple, efficient client. Localisation: material written for one market is not automatically understandable or relevant in another, answered with multilingual and AI-assisted capability. And the boundary of autonomy: they had to decide where AI makes decisions and where human oversight stays valuable, explicitly framing the goal as not eliminating educators and mentors but making personalized support affordable at a scale that would otherwise be expensive.

value.relation: the same pitch at the other end of engineering effort, and the reason this batch is instructive: LearnWay has production clients, a Postgres state machine and four named AI surfaces; Antislop has a PySide shell and a prompt. Neither publishes a learning outcome, so the twelve-field ladder cannot separate them on effect - only the page-substance floor does, which is exactly the distinction the audited-lite tier was built to draw.

the direct competitor in this corpus for the same market, and it holds the answer LearnWay is missing. ax4u sells outputs instead of lessons - an automated workflow, a published book, a deployable system - so 'did the learner acquire a skill' is answered by a deliverable a third party can inspect. LearnWay's loop ends at 'receive feedback'. Read as a pair, the record with the weaker infrastructure has the stronger verification.

the same evidence shape in a different vertical, which is why the lite ladder exists: a shipped, monetised, multi-locale product whose load-bearing model claim is unpublished. Both list localisations as a feature and neither lists an accuracy or outcome figure for the model that the feature depends on.

an instruction that transfers. AttainDesk's year of SMB support work concluded 'less AI, not more'; LearnWay's page argues the opposite direction - AI operating the journey - while agreeing that features are not the measure. The pair frames the open question for every agent-shaped product in this catalog: who evaluates whether the added autonomy helped, and where does that evidence get published.

value: AI-generated quizzes and assessment feedback, which is the capability the whole pivot claims most from and the one with the least published. A generated quiz tests recall of the lesson that was just shown, not whether the skill exists; a generated feedback sentence reads as coaching while grading against a rubric nobody wrote down. Because no accuracy figure, human comparison or rubric is published, there is no way to tell useful feedback from confident feedback - and in a credential-adjacent product that is the failure a learner pays for.

'AI-assisted content workflows' for authoring courses: five words carrying the quality of everything downstream. If generated material enters the library unreviewed, the platform's most important asset becomes unverifiable at the exact scale it is trying to reach, and localisation errors travel with it.

The multilingual claim as stated: Google Cloud Translation localises text, and the page concedes that relevance does not follow from translation. Machine-translated example sentences, currencies, units and cultural references are how a learning product loses credibility with the market it was built for, and no human review step is described anywhere.

Cost per learner at scale. Tutor, mentor, quiz generation and assessment feedback are four inference surfaces per learner per session on a metered-data phone in a market where the whole pitch is price; the page never states a per-learner cost, so the unit economics that decide whether this model survives outside a hackathon are entirely absent.

Deployment claims without an artifact: production Android and iOS apps and a production AI stack are asserted, and neither a store listing, a URL nor a repository is linked, so a reader cannot open what the record is built on. If the store apps are the pre-pivot LearnWay client and the AI layer is not yet shipped to it, the word 'production' is doing two jobs at once.

what_it_does.value: Six named capabilities run through the journey, each attached to a point in it rather than offered as a chat window: an AI Tutor giving contextual explanations while a learner studies; an AI Mentor using goals and progress to recommend what to learn next; AI-powered assessments that evaluate understanding and return actionable feedback; AI-assisted content workflows for authoring material and quizzes; personalised learning pathways through the course catalogue; and multilingual operation across markets. These sit on top of structured courses, practical projects, quizzes, progress tracking and gamification. The stated ambition is the sharp part of the sentence: not a chatbot beside educational content but intelligence embedded through the learner journey, in the shape Learn -> Ask -> Practice -> Assess -> Receive Feedback -> Improve -> Continue.

what_it_is.value: A Flutter and NestJS learning platform for African and other emerging markets that put Gemini into tutoring, mentorship, quiz generation, assessment feedback and pathway choice rather than beside the content - and publishes no learner or outcome figure for any of it.

value: Put the model in the transition, not in a panel. The tutor fires while a learner is stuck mid-lesson, the mentor decides what comes next, the assessment closes the loop; the loop Learn -> Ask -> Practice -> Assess -> Feedback -> Improve -> Continue is the spec. A chatbot beside a video library has the same model and none of the leverage.

Design against the client the user owns, and say so as a constraint: smartphone-only, metered data, cheap hardware, intermittent connectivity. Most AI-edu pitches assume a laptop and a broadband connection and thereby address the learners who least need help.

Treat the pivot as a kept-and-added structure: LearnWay's courses, progress tracking and PostgreSQL state stayed, and the AI layer was built on top of them with that context as input. The alternative - a green-field AI app with no learner state - is why most education demos cannot personalise anything.

Bound the model's authority by the human you are not replacing: 'not to eliminate educators and mentors' is stated as the design objective, which is the honest version of the autonomy debate most records only gesture at.

Instrument the AI features as a first-class product surface - the page says usage and operational data are captured to see how learners interact with them. This is the one hook that could have produced an outcome number, and it is also the caution: telemetry about engagement is not evidence about learning.

learnway-ai.name: LearnWay AI
learnway-ai.tier_note: Lite audit: six fields were established from the page and nothing was read from a repository. Treat `build_is_real` and `stack_consistency` as unexamined, not as passing.
verdict_reasons: soundness 0.41 is too low to certify; stays in the pool
published as audited-lite on 6 of 12 fields (64% of the rubric checkable); the other 6 need a repository or a longer read and are named in `fields_absent`
learnway-ai.worth_note: The geography is the idea. 'AI tutor plus mentor plus assessment' is the most common six-bullet pitch on this shelf - learnway's own competitors in this corpus are lumina-study-buddy, accomplish and antislop - and the page concedes that features are not the measure. What makes LearnWay worth a slot is that it is built for the constraint that breaks the others: phones on mobile data, low-cost devices, tutors who are unavailable at any price, and content that must be localised rather than translated. That is a real design brief and it is the reason this is `niche` and not `tired`. It stops there because not one claim about effect is falsifiable: the record asserts production apps, production AI and continuous improvement, and publishes no learner count, no completion rate, no grading comparison and no repository, while naming the right metric - whether learners achieve better outcomes - without reporting it. Publishing on the lite ladder says exactly that: the page establishes what the product is for and how it is wired, and cannot establish that it works.
